note: Gold-standard scripts per niche. 2 examples each. These are injected into the system prompt as few-shot demonstrations. Every claim is attributable. Every example hits 85-115 words (34-46s at ~150wpm).

finance.seed_content: The stock market is a device for transferring money from the impatient to the patient.
finance.script:
Buffett has owned Coca-Cola stock since 1988.
Thirty-six years. Never sold.
That one position grew from one billion to twenty-five billion dollars.
Not because he picked right. Because he did not move.
The average American investor makes eight trades a year.
Buffett made one major move in the last decade.
Every financial advisor tells you to stay invested long-term.
Almost nobody actually does it when the market drops forty percent.
The skill is not picking the right stock.
The skill is sitting still when everything in you says run.
Still think you need a better strategy?
Follow for daily wealth tactics.

finance.seed_content: Do not look for the needle in the haystack. Just buy the haystack.
finance.script:
The S&P 500 has never been negative over any rolling twenty-year period in history.
Not in 2008. Not during the Great Depression. Not during COVID.
Every single time it came back and went higher.
The average investor underperforms the index by three percent a year.
Not because they picked bad stocks.
Because they sold during the crashes.
Jack Bogle understood this in 1974 and built Vanguard on one idea alone.
Stop trying to beat the market. Buy all of it.
He made more money for ordinary people than any fund manager alive.
The market is not the risk. Your behavior is the risk.
Follow for daily wealth tactics.

motivation.seed_content: We suffer more in imagination than in reality.
motivation.script:
Seneca wrote this two thousand years ago.
We suffer more in imagination than in reality.
He meant the specific thing you are dreading right now.
That conversation you have been putting off for a week.
That decision you keep moving to next Monday.
That call you need to make.
You have been living inside the worst case version of it for days.
Most of the time the actual thing takes five minutes and you wonder what took you so long.
The fear costs more than the thing. Every single time.
What are you rehearsing right now that you just need to do?
Save this. Watch it when you want to quit.

motivation.seed_content: The most important conversations you will ever have are the ones you will have with yourself.
motivation.script:
Goggins ran a hundred miles on two broken feet.
Not because he is superhuman.
Because he spent years training his mind to question its own quit signals.
He says the body stops at forty percent of its actual capacity.
The rest is negotiation.
Not with your legs. With the voice in your head telling you that is enough.
Most people never learn to argue back.
They take the first exit their mind offers and call it a limit.
You have never actually hit your ceiling.
You have only ever believed you did.
When did you last push past the first urge to stop?
Save this. Watch it when you want to quit.

mindset.seed_content: Everything that irritates us about others can lead us to an understanding of ourselves.
mindset.script:
Carl Jung spent decades asking why intelligent people keep making the same mistakes.
His answer: the shadow.
The part of yourself you refuse to look at directly.
When you are furious at someone for being arrogant, check whether you have buried your own ambition.
When you cannot stop judging someone for being weak, check what you are afraid to admit about yourself.
Jung called this projection.
The loudest judgments about others are usually confessions in disguise.
Every strong reaction you have to another person is a map.
The clearest map to your blind spot is your strongest opinion about someone else.
What does your anger tell you about yourself?
This is why one percent think differently.

mindset.seed_content: Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose.
mindset.script:
Viktor Frankl survived three Nazi concentration camps.
He watched people around him break completely. He watched others find meaning in the same conditions.
The difference was not strength. Not luck. Not background.
It was the ability to pause between what happened and how they responded.
Frankl called that pause freedom.
Not freedom from circumstances. Freedom of response.
He said that gap is where your entire character lives.
You cannot control what happens to you.
You can always control the pause before you react.
Most people skip the pause entirely and call the reaction their personality.
Where in your life are you skipping the pause?
This is why one percent think differently.

business.script:
Jeff Bezos built his first competitive strategy around one observation.
Barnes and Noble had thirty to forty percent margins on books in 1995.
Amazon priced books at cost and took losses for three straight years.
By year four, Barnes and Noble could not compete.
They did not lose to better books.
They lost because they had high margins and assumed that made them safe.
Bezos called it the margin opportunity.
Every fat-margin business is telling you exactly where to enter.
Thin margins, high volume, long timeline.
That is how you make an incumbent obsolete without ever having to be better than them.
What high-margin problem in your market still has no cheap solution?
Save this. Build something.

Paul Graham has funded companies worth over one trillion dollars combined.
He has one test he applies to every founder in the first ten minutes.
Not the idea. Not the market size. Not the team credentials.
One question: do you talk to your users every week?
Most founders build for six months then wonder why nobody wants it.
Graham's answer is always the same.
You cannot build what people want from inside a room.
You have to go ask them what keeps them up at night and build exactly that.
Dropbox, Airbnb, Stripe. All of them started by talking to ten people.
When did you last talk directly to someone who needs what you are building?
Save this. Build something.

personal_development.seed_content: You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.
personal_development.script:
James Clear spent three years studying why people fail to build habits.
His one finding that changed everything: you do not rise to your goals. You fall to your systems.
A goal to run a marathon will not get you out of bed on a Tuesday in February.
Running shoes already placed on the mat the night before will.
The difference is not motivation.
It is the number of decisions required to start.
Remove the decision. The habit runs itself.
He sold ten million copies of one book on this single idea.
Identity over outcome. System over goal. Process over result.
What is one decision you could eliminate from tomorrow morning?
Do this tomorrow morning.

personal_development.seed_content: Specific knowledge is found by pursuing your genuine curiosity, not whatever is hot right now.
personal_development.script:
Naval Ravikant built two companies, invested in Twitter, Uber, and Notion early, and retired at forty.
He has one piece of advice he keeps repeating.
Do not optimize for what is hot. Optimize for what you cannot stop thinking about.
He calls it specific knowledge.
The kind of expertise that looks like play to you and work to everyone else.
That asymmetry is a competitive advantage you cannot replicate with discipline alone.
You cannot fake genuine curiosity. The market eventually figures it out.
People who followed trends are doing okay.
People who followed obsessions built the companies everyone else wishes they had started.
What do you keep coming back to that you have been calling a distraction?
Do this tomorrow morning.
